issues.issue: Undefined capitalized terms are imported from the Pooling and Servicing Agreement, a document not attached, so terms actually used in the operative text such as "Material Defect" and "MOM Loan" in Section 6(a) have no meaning within this instrument. A court would have to decide whether the PSA definitions govern and what happens where none exists.

The definition uses the shorthand "Accredited" as a defined party although that term is nowhere defined in this Agreement. Its referent must be inferred from Exhibit C of the attached Underlying EMC Purchase Agreement.
"Accredited" is used as though defined but no definition of that entity appears in this Agreement. The class of Accredited Mortgage Loans therefore depends on an undefined identifier.

The dollar figures for the Acquisition Price are blank or garbled ("cash in an amount equal to $ i"; "an amount equal to of"), so the price term cannot be read off the instrument. A court asked to fix the consideration would have nothing in the text to work with.

"Covered" is defined only by reference to Appendix E of Standard & Poor's Glossary, an external and undated document whose content the parties do not reproduce. Which version of that glossary governs is left open.

Section 2(a) requires each Mortgage Loan Seller to sell loans with an aggregate Cut-off Date balance "equal to the Cut-off Date Balance," yet this definition fixes a single pool-wide figure. Read together the two provisions cannot both be satisfied by two sellers.
The definition breaks off mid-phrase with an unclosed quotation ("in such capacity, the “Custodian"), leaving the defined term incomplete on its face.

This definition and the Wells Fargo Custodial Agreement definition both define "Custodian," so the single term carries two different referents in the same definitional section. Provisions referring to "the related Custodian" must be construed to pick between them.

"Scheduled Payment" is used in the definition but is not defined in this Agreement; the operative provisions elsewhere speak of "Monthly Payment." The reader must import a term from the Pooling and Servicing Agreement to apply it.

An "EMC Mortgage Loan" is defined by who sold it, while "MSMCH Represented Mortgage Loans" is defined by who originated it, so a loan sold by EMC can also be a loan MSMCH represents upon. The overlap leaves it uncertain which seller's warranty regime governs such a loan.

The catch-all "or similar loan under any other applicable state, federal or local law" sits against the enumerated labels "high cost home," "threshold," "covered," "high risk home" and "predatory," so its reach is uncertain under ejusdem generis. Whether a given state statute produces a "similar" loan is a question the words do not answer.

The phrase "creating a first or second lien on or first or second priority ownership interest in an estate in fee simple in real property" is grammatically tangled and confines Mortgages to fee simple estates. Whether leasehold-secured or co-op loans qualify cannot be read off the words.

The definition is left indefinite on its face — "certain" loans "and certain other assets as described in the Prospectus Supplement" — so the population of Mortgage Loans is fixed only by an external offering document. What "certain other assets" are included cannot be determined from the Agreement.
Item (29) reads "a code indicating whether the Mortgage Loan is has a balloon payment," a plain drafting error in an enumerated data field.

This 33-item definition of the Mortgage Loan Schedule does not match the 25-item list in Exhibit 2, to which Section 3 directs the parties for the schedule's contents. The two lists differ in substance (e.g. street address and Mortgagor's name appear only in Exhibit 2), so what the schedule must contain is contested.

The definition says the rate is that "borne by a Mortgage Note as stated herein," but no rate is stated in this Agreement; the drafter plainly meant "therein," i.e., in the Mortgage Note. The error makes the definition circular as written.

The class is defined by originator (Aames, Aegis, Decision One, First NLC, MILA, New Century, Option One, Wilmington) and so excludes Fremont and Accredited loans, yet Section 10(b)(18) and the Accredited backstop paragraph purport to make representations within Section 10(b) about exactly those excluded loans. The scope of MSMCH's warranty obligation cannot be reconciled across those provisions.
"Piggyback Loan" is defined but the term appears nowhere in the operative provisions of this Agreement, leaving the definition without work to do.

Clause (iii) is garbled — "in connection with any violation of such Mortgage Loan of any anti-predatory lending laws" — so the costs and damages component of the repurchase price is hard to apply as written.

The definition conditions substitution on "the requirements stated herein," but this Agreement states no eligibility requirements for a Replacement Mortgage Loan anywhere; only the Underlying EMC Purchase Agreement's "Qualified Substitute Mortgage Loan" definition supplies criteria. Whether those criteria govern the substitution right in Section 10 is left open.

The definition describes the Underlying EMC Purchase Agreement as "between EMC and MSMCH," but the agreement actually attached as Exhibit 3 is between EMC and Morgan Stanley Mortgage Capital Inc., a different entity from Morgan Stanley Mortgage Capital Holdings LLC. Which document and which counterparty is meant is a genuine question.

"Value" is defined here as the lesser of appraisal and sales price, while the representations in Section 10 turn on "Appraised Value," defined in the attached Underlying EMC Purchase Agreement simply as the appraisal figure. The two valuation standards sit side by side without a rule of priority.

This definition designates Wells Fargo as "the Custodian" while the Deutsche Bank Custodial Agreement definition gives the same defined term to Deutsche Bank. References elsewhere to "the related Custodian" must be construed to resolve the duplication.

The obligation is keyed to loans "having an aggregate outstanding principal balance as of the Cut-off Date equal to the Cut-off Date Balance" for each Mortgage Loan Seller, although the Cut-off Date Balance is one pool-wide number; it also sells an interest in "the Swap Agreements," a term never defined. Both leave the sale obligation indeterminate.

The condition precedent is "the conditions set forth in Section 11 hereof," but Section 11 assigns the Accredited and Fremont letters and contains no conditions; the closing conditions are in Section 14. The cross-reference must be construed or corrected.

Payment of the Acquisition Price is made conditional on "the conditions set forth in Section 11 hereof," but Section 11 contains no conditions; the closing conditions appear in Section 14. A court would have to decide whether the payment obligation is conditioned at all.

Section 3 directs that the Mortgage Loan Schedule set forth "the information listed on Exhibit 2," while the Section 1 definition of Mortgage Loan Schedule prescribes a different 33-item list. The required content of the schedule cannot be determined without choosing between them.

The obligation is imposed on "EMC or MSMCH, as applicable," but the cost is allocated "at EMC's own expense," so the text makes EMC bear a cost of MSMCH's performance. Which party pays when MSMCH performs cannot be read off the words.

The paragraph recites that "the Master Servicer agrees that it will not" alter the MERS codes, yet the Master Servicer is not a party to this Agreement (see the preamble naming only EMC, MSMCH and the Purchaser). Whether that undertaking binds anyone here is left open.

The due diligence obligation is measured by "such due diligence as any such party reasonably believes is appropriate," a standard set by the requesting party's own belief with no external benchmark. Its outer limit is not stated.

The paragraph imposes affirmative duties on the Trustee to assign loans and execute transfer instruments, but the Trustee is not a party to this Agreement under the preamble. Whether those duties are enforceable here, or only under the Pooling and Servicing Agreement, is a live question.

The text breaks off mid-sentence ("shall be submitted for recording ... at no expense to" followed immediately by "Certificates evidencing Percentage Interests aggregating not less than 25% of the Trust"), and the enumerated list contains two clauses numbered "(iv)." The recording exception cannot be applied as written.

The paragraph directs that on failure to record "the provisions of Section 5(c) and (d) shall apply," but Section 5 of this Agreement has only subsections (a) and (b), and "Material Defect" is defined nowhere in the instrument. The consequence of a recording failure therefore has no operative referent.
The final clause reads "and EMC not in default with respect to any order of any court," omitting the verb "is," so the sentence is ungrammatical as a warranty.

The warranty is given about "the Mortgage Loan Seller's Information (as defined in Section 14(a) hereof)," but Section 14(a) sets out closing conditions and defines no such term anywhere in the Agreement. The subject matter of this disclosure warranty is therefore unidentified.

EMC's only loan-level warranty appears here, yet no cure, repurchase or substitution remedy is provided for its breach — the remedy paragraph in Section 10 runs only against MSMCH, while Section 19 declares the Trustee's sole remedy to be obligations "contained in Sections 5 and 7," which contain none. What follows a breach by EMC cannot be determined from the instrument.

This warranty is given "with respect to each Mortgage Loan," including loans sold by EMC, while the remedy paragraph of Section 10 obliges MSMCH to cure, purchase or substitute only as to "MSMCH Represented Mortgage Loans." Whether MSMCH warrants the whole pool, and with what consequence, is genuinely contestable.

The compliance warranty extends to "each Mortgage Loan," but the cure/repurchase machinery later in Section 10 is limited to MSMCH Represented Mortgage Loans as defined in Section 1. The scope of MSMCH's exposure for EMC-sold loans cannot be settled without construing the two together.

"No Mortgage Loan is a High Cost Loan or Covered Loan, as applicable" leaves the qualifier "as applicable" without a referent, and the date formula "originated on or after October 1, 2002 through March 6, 2003" is awkwardly bounded. Both make the warranty's coverage uncertain at its edges.

The permitted-encumbrance list ends with the catch-all "other matters to which like properties are commonly subject which do not materially interfere with the benefits of the security," set against three specific enumerated exceptions. How far that residual category reaches is the sort of general-versus-specific question the words do not resolve.

The warranty turns on the Mortgage containing "customary and enforceable provisions such as to render the rights and remedies of the holder thereof adequate," a standard whose content ("customary," "adequate") is nowhere fixed. Whether a given form of mortgage satisfies it is not answerable from the text.

The sentence "unless at the time of the ... origination, such Mortgagor did not qualify taking into such facts as, without limitation, ..." omits a word (plainly "account") and the qualification test it states cannot be parsed. The warranty's condition is unintelligible as written.

This warranty is given "solely with respect to the Fremont Mortgage Loans ... and Accredited Mortgage Loans," yet subsection (b) in which it sits is expressly limited to MSMCH Represented Mortgage Loans, a defined class that excludes Fremont and Accredited originations. The two cannot be harmonised without deciding which controls.

The warranty requires the appraiser to have been "duly appointed by MSMCH," but the MSMCH Represented Mortgage Loans are by definition loans originated by third parties whose appraisers MSMCH did not appoint. The representation cannot be true as literally worded for the class it covers.

"LTV" is used without definition in this Agreement; the attached Underlying EMC Purchase Agreement defines "Loan-to-Value Ratio" by a formula that itself turns on a choice between appraised value and purchase price. How the 100% test is computed is therefore unfixed.

The paragraph deems the Section 10 warranties to be remade "by the related Mortgage Loan Seller" on substitution, although Section 10 contains only MSMCH's warranties and EMC's separate warranty appears in Section 8. Whether EMC is thereby made to give the Section 10 representations is a genuine question.

The clause lists three responses — "(i) cure such breach ..., (ii) purchase the affected Mortgage Loan ... or (iii) ... substitute" — without saying who elects among them, and then declares those obligations the "sole and exclusive remedy under this Agreement or otherwise." Whether the seller or the purchaser chooses, and how far "or otherwise" reaches, are both open on the words.

The remedy is confined to breaches affecting "MSMCH Represented Mortgage Loans," while Section 10(a) makes MSMCH's warranties as to "each Mortgage Loan" in the pool. Breaches of Section 10(a) as to non-represented loans are left with no stated remedy.

The paragraph speaks of "a breach of a representation or warranty set forth in this Section 10 made by Accredited," but Accredited makes no representations in Section 10 — its warranties live in a separate assignment, assumption and recognition agreement. The trigger for MSMCH's backstop obligation is thus described inaccurately.

MSMCH's backstop runs to Accredited Mortgage Loans, but Accredited-originated loans fall outside the defined class of MSMCH Represented Mortgage Loans to which the preceding remedy paragraph is limited. Whether the 90-day cure/purchase machinery applies to them at all must be construed.

The clause purports to fix when a cause of action "shall accrue" — on discovery or notice plus failure to cure or repurchase — which can be read either as a condition precedent to suit or as an attempt to postpone the running of limitations. That choice determines whether claims are timely and is not settled by the words.

Accrual is stated only "as to any MSMCH Represented Mortgage Loan," although the sentence opens by covering breaches of "any representations and warranties made in this Section 10," which under Section 10(a) reach each Mortgage Loan. The two halves of the sentence do not cover the same loans.

Sections 2(a), 2(c) and 20 all treat Section 11 as containing the conditions to closing, but Section 11 is an assignment of the Accredited agreement and the Fremont bring-down letter and states no conditions. The instrument cannot be read coherently until that mismatch is resolved.

The condition refers to Certificates sold "pursuant to the Underwriting Agreement and the Purchase Agreement," but "the Purchase Agreement" is not a defined term anywhere in this instrument. Which document is meant cannot be told from the text.

"EMC and MSMCH shall pay fees and expenses as previously agreed" identifies neither the fees nor the agreement fixing them, so the allocation of costs is indefinite on the face of the clause. Which expenses fall within it cannot be determined from the words.

The clause depends on a prior, unwritten arrangement, yet Section 29 declares this Agreement the entire agreement and "supersedes all prior and contemporaneous agreements ... oral or written." The two provisions pull in opposite directions.

The facsimile number given for EMC ("241-626-4714") is malformed and differs from the EMC fax number in the attached Underlying EMC Purchase Agreement, which could matter to whether notice was validly given.

The clause makes the Trustee's sole remedy "the cure, purchase or substitution obligations contained in Sections 5 and 7 hereof," but those obligations are in Section 10; Sections 5 and 7 are examination of mortgage files and EMC's corporate representations. It also preserves for the Purchaser benefits "set forth in Sections 12, 14 and 18," although Section 12 is reserved and Section 18 is a notice provision.

Termination rights are keyed to "the conditions ... set forth under Section 11(a)" and "Section 11(b)," but Section 11 has subsections (a) and (b) that assign two agreements and contain no closing conditions; the conditions are in Section 14(a) and (b). The termination right cannot be exercised as written without correcting the reference.

Section 26 obliges the parties to carry out "any amendments hereto which may be required by either Rating Agency," while this section forbids amendment without the prior written consent of each party. Whether a rating-agency-driven amendment can be compelled turns on reconciling the two.

The obligation to take actions "including any amendments hereto which may be required by either Rating Agency" sits against Section 24, which bars any amendment without each party's prior written consent. A party could read this section as compelling the very consent Section 24 makes optional.

The section extends the benefit of the Agreement to Bear Stearns "to the extent specified in Section 14 hereof," but Section 14 (conditions to closing) confers nothing on Bear Stearns; the provisions naming Bear Stearns are in Section 5(a). The extent of Bear Stearns' rights is therefore unascertainable from the reference given.

The clause supersedes all prior agreements on the subject matter, yet Section 15 makes the parties' fee obligations turn on terms "as previously agreed" and the Agreement elsewhere depends on the attached Underlying EMC Purchase Agreement. Whether those prior arrangements survive is a real question.

The enumeration is corrupted — item (ii) is followed by a second, unbracketed "ii)" — and item (v) reads "Verification of © acceptable evidence of source and amount of downpayment." The list of required file contents is not cleanly stated.

This exhibit defines the Mortgage File as containing only "copies of the Mortgage Loan Documents" and ancillary papers, while Section 4(b) requires delivery of original Mortgages, original assignments and, in lieu of original Mortgage Notes, lost note affidavits. What the seller actually had to deliver cannot be settled from the exhibit alone.

The closing sentence requires "the total of each of the amounts described under (0) above," but item (o) is the Interest Rate Adjustment Date, which is a date and cannot be totalled; the drafter plainly meant item (n), the principal balances. The aggregation requirement is unworkable as written.

This 25-item exhibit list differs from the 33-item definition of "Mortgage Loan Schedule" in Section 1, which Section 3 nevertheless equates with the Exhibit 2 information. The required contents of the schedule are stated twice and inconsistently.

The attached agreement is between EMC and Morgan Stanley Mortgage Capital Inc., but the Mortgage Loan Purchase Agreement defines the "Underlying EMC Purchase Agreement" as one "between EMC and MSMCH" (Morgan Stanley Mortgage Capital Holdings LLC). The identity of the counterparty whose warranties were assigned is therefore contested on the face of the papers.

"Accepted Servicing Practices" is defined circularly by reference to "accepted mortgage servicing practices of prudent mortgage lending institutions," a standard with no fixed content. Whether particular servicing conduct complies cannot be answered from the words.

"Appraised Value" is simply the appraisal figure here, while the Loan-to-Value Ratio definition and the Mortgage Loan Purchase Agreement's "Value" definition take the lesser of appraisal and purchase price. The valuation input for the LTV warranties depends on which of these controls.

The definition requires every Assignment of Mortgage to be "in recordable form and in blank," while Exhibit A-1(e) provides that if the assignment is to be recorded "the Mortgage shall be assigned to the Purchaser" and only otherwise delivered in blank. The two cannot both be satisfied for a recorded assignment.

The Closing Date is fixed as a single date, but Sections 9 and 10 repeatedly speak of "each Closing Date" and "the initial Closing Date," contemplating more than one. Whether further closings were possible turns on reconciling the definition with those sections.

The denominator is "the Appraised Value as determined pursuant to the Underwriting Guidelines," but "Underwriting Guidelines" is not a defined term in this Agreement and Appraised Value is separately defined without reference to any guidelines. The computation cannot be performed as written.
"Covered" is fixed only by Appendix E of Standard & Poor's Glossary, an undated external document that the parties do not reproduce. Which edition governs is not stated.
The definition reads "repurchased or to be repurchase or replaced," a plain grammatical error in the operative phrase identifying which loans are Deleted Mortgage Loans.

A payment is "Delinquent" here as soon as it is unpaid at the next Due Date, yet the loan-level warranties speak of payments "not yet 30 days Delinquent" and of being "30 days or more Delinquent." Stacking a day-count on this definition produces an ambiguous measure of delinquency.

The definition is truncated mid-sentence — "A Mortgage Loan secured by the pledge of stock allocated toa" — so what constitutes a Co-op Loan is not stated. Provisions that turn on Co-op Loan status have no complete definition to apply.

The Group 1 originator list (including Meritage and NC Capital) does not line up with the originators listed in the Mortgage Loan Purchase Agreement's definition of MSMCH Represented Mortgage Loans, although both purport to mark out the loans carrying seller-level warranties. Which loans carry which warranty set is not settled by either list alone.

The catch-all "or similar loan under any other applicable state, federal or local law" follows a list of specific statutory labels, leaving its reach to be settled by ejusdem generis. Whether a loan is "similar" to a "threshold" or "high risk home" loan is not answered by the text.

The Letter Agreement is between Morgan Stanley & Co. Incorporated and Bear, Stearns & Co. Inc. — neither of them a party to this Agreement — yet it fixes the Purchase Price Percentage on which Section 4 and the Repurchase Price depend. Whether its terms bind these parties is a real question.

The first sentence defines the Lifetime Rate Cap as a "provision" of the Mortgage Note, while the second states a substantive rate limit by reference to "the amount per annum set forth on the Mortgage Loan Schedule." The defined term therefore denotes both a clause and a number.

The denominator is "the lesser of (a) the Appraised Value ... and (b) if the Mortgage Loan was made to finance the acquisition ..., the purchase price," but for a refinancing there is no item (b), so the "lesser of" formula has only one term. How the ratio is computed for non-purchase loans is not stated.

The definition limits a Mortgage to an instrument "which creates a first lien on the Mortgaged Property," yet the Agreement expressly covers Second Lien Loans, defined as loans "secured by a second lien Mortgage," and the Exhibit F warranties address second liens throughout. On its own terms a second-lien loan has no qualifying Mortgage.

This definition limits the Exhibit A-2 items to those "in the possession of the applicable Servicer," while Exhibit A-2 itself limits them to items "in the possession of the applicable Seller." The two possession qualifiers cannot both be right.

"Mortgage Interest Rate Cap" and "Periodic Rate Cap" are separately defined to describe the same per-adjustment limit in the Mortgage Note, and the Qualified Substitute Mortgage Loan test uses only the former. Which definition governs a substitution test is not settled.

Mortgaged Property here extends to leasehold estates and co-op stock, while the companion "Mortgage" definition requires an instrument creating a first lien on that property and the Mortgage Loan Purchase Agreement's "Mortgage" definition requires an estate in fee simple. The classes of eligible collateral do not line up.

The sentence "the absolute maximum amount by which the Mortgage Interest Rate there may increase or decrease" contains a stray word and is ungrammatical, and the definition then equates the Cap with "the rate set forth as such on the Mortgage Loan Schedule." The term denotes both a note provision and a schedule figure.

The whole price term is fixed by the Letter Agreement, a document between Morgan Stanley & Co. Incorporated and Bear, Stearns & Co. Inc. rather than the parties to this Agreement, and it also drives the Repurchase Price. Whether that outside document supplies an enforceable price here is genuinely open.

A Qualified Appraiser must be "duly appointed by the Seller," but the Mortgage Loans were originated by third-party Originators and merely purchased by the Seller, so no appraiser on those loans was appointed by the Seller. The appraisal warranty in Exhibit F cannot be satisfied on a literal reading.
"Qualified Correspondent" is elaborately defined but the term is used nowhere in the operative provisions or exhibits of this Agreement, leaving the definition without effect.
The definition ends "or their respective successors designated by the Purchasers," using a plural where the Agreement has a single Purchaser. It is unclear whose designation is required.

Component (b) reads "the accrued interest on such Stated Principal Balance at the Mortgage Interest Rate from the last interest paid to date through which interest has been paid ... through the date prior to the date of repurchase," a doubled and garbled formula for the interest period. The amount payable on repurchase cannot be computed with confidence from the words.

The closing words "none of which is a mobile home" trail a six-item list, so it is unclear whether the exclusion qualifies only Manufactured Homes or every category. The boundary between a Manufactured Home and a mobile home is also left unstated.

The Servicer is to be identified on Exhibit B, but Section 7 directs the reader to "the Mortgage Loan Schedule attached as Exhibit C" for the same information, and Exhibit C is the schedule of Prior Purchase and Servicing Agreements. The source of the servicer designation is inconsistently stated.

Servicing Rights are excluded from the conveyance by Subsection 6.01 and include Escrow Payments, late fees and amounts collected by the Seller, yet Subsection 6.02 vests in the Purchaser "all rights arising out of the Mortgage Loans including ... all funds received by the Seller ... after the Cut-off Date." The two provisions allocate the same collections to different parties.

The quantity sold is "an amount set forth on the Mortgage Loan Schedule," but Exhibit B, where that schedule is to be attached, states only "Provided Upon Request." The subject matter of the sale cannot be identified from the instrument itself.

The Purchase Price turns entirely on the Purchase Price Percentage, which is "set forth in the Letter Agreement" between Morgan Stanley & Co. Incorporated and Bear, Stearns & Co. Inc. — neither a party here. The price cannot be computed from this Agreement alone.

The Purchaser takes principal from the Cut-off Date (June 1, 2007) but interest only "from and after the Closing Date," which the definitions fix as May 31, 2007 — a closing that precedes the cut-off. The allocation of the June interest and principal cannot be squared with those two dates.

This subsection assigns the Prior Purchase Agreements "except with respect to the Group 1 Mortgage Loans," yet Subsection 8.02 states flatly that the Purchaser "shall be the assignee of the representations and warranties of the related Originator ... as described in Subsection 6.01." Whether the Purchaser obtained originator recourse on Group 1 loans is left unresolved.

This subsection vests in the Purchaser "all rights arising out of the Mortgage Loans including ... all funds received by the Seller ... after the Cut-off Date," while Subsection 6.01 excludes the Servicing Rights from the conveyance and the definition of Servicing Rights captures late fees, Escrow Payments and amounts collected by the Seller. The same collections are allocated twice.

The paragraph ends in garbled and incomplete text — "and a asa a sale of assets 0 on the" — so the accounting-treatment covenant is cut off mid-sentence. What the Seller and Purchaser had to record cannot be read from the clause.

The final sentence puts all custodian fees on the Purchaser, while Section 11 allocates costs between the parties and puts "all other costs and expenses incurred in connection with the transfer and delivery" on the Purchaser subject to specified Seller items. The two cost provisions overlap without a stated priority.

The loans are said to be sold "on a servicing retained basis," yet the next paragraph requires the Seller to assign each Servicing Agreement to the Purchaser and to have the servicers service "for the Purchaser." What the Seller retained is not clear from the two paragraphs read together.

The paragraph directs the reader to "the Mortgage Loan Schedule attached as Exhibit C," but the Mortgage Loan Schedule is defined and attached as Exhibit B, and Exhibit C is the schedule of Prior Purchase and Servicing Agreements. Which document identifies the governing servicing arrangement is uncertain.

The sentence duplicates its verb — "No consent ... is required for the transactions ... from any court ... having jurisdiction over the Seller is required" — leaving the warranty ungrammatical. Its scope is blurred by the doubled construction.

The warranty is framed as a double negative — the Seller "does not believe, nor does it have any reason or cause to believe, that it cannot perform" — so what state of affairs is warranted is hard to pin down. It gives no objective standard of ability to perform.

The Purchaser is made assignee of the Originators' Representations and Warranties "as described in Subsection 6.01," but Subsection 6.01 expressly excludes the Prior Purchase Agreements for Group 1 Mortgage Loans from the assignment. The two provisions describe different assignments.

The sentence runs "within 120 days of the earlier of either discovery by or receipt of notice by the Seller of the breach ... the Seller shall take such actions as described in the following paragraph," with conditions (1) and (2) embedded so that the subject and the 120-day period cannot be cleanly matched. Whether the 120 days is a cure window or a deadline to act is not clear on the face of it.

The paragraph states overlapping and inconsistent triggers: the Seller must cure and "if such breach cannot be cured" repurchase at the Purchaser's option, but the next sentence gives a 120-day cure period and the third a 180-day substitution window keyed to the Closing Date. Which timetable governs a given breach cannot be read off the words.

The indemnity is available only "provided the Mortgage Loans are not the subject of a Reconstitution," yet Section 12 exists precisely to effect a Reconstitution of these loans into a securitization, which would extinguish the indemnity the same clause then calls part of the Purchaser's "sole remedies." The two provisions cannot comfortably be read together.

The clause fixes when a cause of action "shall accrue" — on discovery or notice plus failure to cure or repurchase — which may be read as a condition precedent to suit or as an attempt to postpone the limitations period. That choice decides timeliness and is not resolved by the words.

Accrual here is triggered by "discovery of such breach by the Purchaser or the Servicer or notice thereof by the Seller," while the Subsection 8.02 trigger paragraph runs from "discovery by or receipt of notice by the Seller." The two paragraphs identify different discovering parties for the same breach.

"FPD" is defined in Section 1 as "first payment default provisions ... as described in Subsection 8.03," but this subsection describes no such provisions and instead points onward to the Prior Purchase Agreements. The definition is circular and the triggering default event is never stated.

This section speaks of a single "Closing Date" while the immediately following conditions and Section 10 refer to "each Closing Date" and to "the initial Closing Date," contemplating multiple closings. Whether more than one closing was possible turns on which reading prevails.

The enumeration is scrambled — the markers "(iv)" and "(v)" appear in the middle of clause (iii) and their text follows afterwards — so the closing conditions cannot be matched to their numbers as printed. The list also closes with an open-ended condition that "all other terms and conditions of this Agreement (unless waived) shall have been complied with."

The list of closing documents is numbered "1." and then simply runs on without numbers for the remaining four items, so the enumeration is broken. The set of required originals must be inferred from the run-on text.

This paragraph contemplates a Reconstitution "on one or more dates (each, a 'Reconstitution Date')" of "some or all" of the loans, while the next paragraph limits the Purchaser to a single Reconstitution. The two sentences pull against each other.

This caps the Purchaser at "one (1) Reconstitution," but Section 18 states that "the Purchaser shall be limited to three (3) assignments or transfers with respect to the Mortgage Loans and this Agreement as described in Section 12." The two limits on the same transfers are irreconcilable.

This paragraph obliges the Seller to repurchase or substitute "as if it were the related Originator" whenever an Originator fails to remedy a breach, without the 120-day machinery or the "sole remedies" limit of Subsection 8.02. Whether the Subsection 8.02 conditions and remedy cap apply to this backstop is unresolved.

The closing sentence declares all of the Purchaser's rights and remedies "distinct from, and cumulative with, any other rights or remedies ... afforded by law or equity," while Subsection 8.02 states that cure, substitution, repurchase and indemnity "constitute the sole remedies of the Purchaser" for warranty breaches. The two remedy provisions directly contradict each other.

The section insists the transaction is a true sale and not a debt instrument, while Section 13 has the Seller grant the Purchaser "a lien on and a continuing security interest in each Mortgage Loan" and hold the loans in custody. A court asked to characterise the transfer would have to reconcile the two.

This section limits the Purchaser to "three (3) assignments or transfers with respect to the Mortgage Loans and this Agreement as described in Section 12," but Section 12 limits the Purchaser to one Reconstitution. The permitted number of transfers is stated twice and differently.

The covenant turns on what it is to "solicit a Mortgagor ... for the purpose of refinancing," a term the section never defines and whose boundary is then cut back by two carve-outs. Whether particular marketing crosses the line is the classic question this wording leaves open.

Exception (i) reads "so long as such promotional material either is sent to the mortgagors for all of the mortgages in the servicing portfolio ..." — the word "either" has no matching alternative, so one limb of the safe harbour is missing. The scope of the permitted advertising cannot be determined.

The prescribed endorsement is quoted with a blank payee — "Pay to the order of , Without recourse" — so the required form of endorsement is incomplete on the face of the exhibit. Whether a note endorsed in blank satisfies item (a) is left open.

Item (e) requires the original Assignment of Mortgage "in form and substance acceptable for recording" and, if recorded, assigned to the Purchaser, whereas the Section 1 definition of Assignment of Mortgage requires every such assignment to be "in recordable form and in blank." The delivery standard is stated two ways.

This exhibit limits the listed items to those "in the possession of the applicable Seller," while the Section 1 definition of Mortgage File limits the same Exhibit A-2 items to those in the possession of "the applicable Servicer." The contents of the Mortgage File differ depending on which is read.

The form assigns all of the Purchase Agreements insofar as they relate to the Mortgage Loans, whereas Subsection 6.01 of the Mortgage Loan Purchase and Warranties Agreement excludes the Prior Purchase Agreements for Group 1 Mortgage Loans from the assignment. Which loans' originator recourse actually passed cannot be settled from this clause alone.

The Assignor warrants that "attached hereto as Exhibit B are true and accurate copies of the Purchase Agreements," but Exhibit B in the executed document is a blank page bearing only its caption. What was warranted as attached cannot be identified.

The Assignor warrants that Exhibit C contains "true and accurate copies of the Servicing Agreements," but the Exhibit C attached to this form is a blank captioned page. The subject of the warranty is missing from the instrument.

The sentence doubles its operative verb — "No consent ... is required for the transactions contemplated by this Agreement from any court ... having jurisdiction over the Assignor is required" — leaving the warranty ungrammatical as written.

The warranty concerns the Assignor's right to "assign its rights in the Agreements," but "the Agreements" is capitalised without ever being defined in this instrument, which defines only "Purchase Agreements" and "Servicing Agreements." Its reach is therefore uncertain.

This priority clause makes the assignment agreement control over "the Purchase Agreements or the Servicing Agreements" as to the Mortgage Loans, yet the whole scheme of Subsection 8.02 depends on the Purchaser taking the Originators' representations and remedies as they stand in those Purchase Agreements. Which document governs a warranty dispute turns on reading the two together.

The list of permitted prior interests is corrupted: item (2) has lost its text and survives only as the stray word "payable;", so one of the exceptions to the lien warranty is missing. The clause also ends with an open catch-all for "other matters to which like properties are commonly subject."

The warranty is made "subject only to the exceptions contained in clauses (1), (2) and (3) of paragraph (e) of this Exhibit F," but the Exhibit uses upper-case letters and the corresponding paragraph (E) has lost the text of clause (2) altogether. The permitted title exceptions cannot be identified.

The carve-out is "except as set forth in paragraph (b) above," but paragraph (B) is the No Defenses warranty; the delinquency carve-out this clause needs sits in paragraph (A), Payments Current. The exception points to the wrong provision.

The warranty rests on the Mortgage containing "customary and enforceable provisions such as to render the rights and remedies of the holder thereof adequate," with neither "customary" nor "adequate" given content. Compliance cannot be tested against the words.

Text is missing from the middle of the warranty — "The Mortgaged Property is undamaged by waste, fire, adversely the value of the Mortgaged Property as security" — so the list of casualties and the materiality qualifier have dropped out. What condition of the property was warranted cannot be read from the clause.

The qualification test reads "such Mortgagor did not qualify taking into such facts as, without limitation, ...", omitting a word and leaving the sentence unparseable. Because a breach of this clause (N) is deemed automatically material under Subsection 8.02, its meaning matters.

"No Mortgage Loan is a High Cost Loan or Covered Loan, as applicable" leaves "as applicable" without a referent, and the phrase "originated on or after October 1, 2002 through March 6, 2003" states its window awkwardly. The reach of a warranty whose breach is deemed automatically material is thereby blurred.

The Seller warrants it is "the sole owner of record and holder" of each Mortgage Loan, while Subsection 6.02 contemplates that record title may stand in the name of an Affiliate of the Seller or of MERS as nominee. The two statements about record ownership do not match.

The appraiser must be a Qualified Appraiser "duly appointed by the Seller," but the recitals establish that the Seller bought these loans from third-party Originators, whose appraisers it did not appoint. On a literal reading the warranty could never be satisfied.

The heading is mistyped ("LIV") and the warranty uses "LTV," a term this Agreement never defines; the defined measure is "Loan-to-Value Ratio," which itself has a two-limb denominator. How the 100% test is applied is not fixed by the text.

The warranty is that each loan's characteristics "conform to the securitization requirements and loan level representations and warranties that are consistent with those applicable to a securitization transaction" of a described hypothetical kind, a standard with no ascertainable content. Because breach of this clause (D) triggers a repurchase obligation under Subsection 8.03, its vagueness is operative.
